families.axis_name: From self-assertive independence to chosen interdependence
families.decision_variable: When her own ambitions and freedom conflict with close relationships, does Jo act to preserve personal autonomy or to bind herself through shared duty and reciprocal care?

phase_contrasts.contrast: She shifts from chiefly protecting her independence against domestic claims to voluntarily using her will in concrete service to family needs.
She moves from duty accepted as immediate family obligation to testing whether work, ambition, and honesty can stand on their own without yielding to unwanted relational claims.
She shifts from guarding self-direction against binding attachments to deliberately choosing a life organized around mutual love, caregiving, and shared labor.

axis_re_expression.abstract_axis: How a person organizes autonomy and self-determination in relation to attachment, obligation, and reciprocal care.
abstract_phases: Defiant autonomy against imposed affiliation
Self-directed competence channeled into responsibility
Independent striving constrained by loss and relational limits
Freely chosen interdependence through generative care

0.rationale: In chapters 1–5, Jo's resistance to feminine roles, longing to be a boy, and spirited peer bond with Laurie fit a mid-adolescent stage of identity assertion and rebellion against constraint.

1.rationale: Across chapters 6–18, Jo is still in late adolescence, but her independence is being shaped by family duty through household work, caring for Beth, and supporting Marmee.

2.rationale: In chapters 19–35, Jo moves into young adulthood as she pursues paid writing, wrestles with marriage proposals and family transitions, and confronts grief that complicates her ambitions.

3.rationale: Across chapters 36–47, marriage, building Plumfield, caregiving, and teaching clearly place Jo in young adulthood, where her agency is integrated into chosen interdependent adult life.

probes.scenario: At home with her sisters, Meg begins scolding Jo for boyish tricks and says that, now she is tall and wears her hair up, she ought to behave like a young lady. Beth and Amy are present as the rebuke lands.
probes.question: How does Josephine March answer being told to leave off boyish ways and act like a young lady?

phase_responses.gt_action: She yanks off her hair net, shakes down her hair, and rattles the blue army-sock in angry protest.
phase_responses.gt_speech: I'm not! and if turning up my hair makes me one, I'll wear it in two tails till I'm twenty,
phase_responses.gt_thought: Being called a young lady feels like a sentence, not a compliment. She hears grown-up femininity as a trap that keeps her from freedom, usefulness, and the life she wants.

voice.note: This fits Jo in chapter 1: the hair-net gesture, the blue army-sock, and the protest against being made into a 'young lady' all sound true to her rebellious, boyish resistance, and the thought uses period-plausible ideas without reaching beyond what she knows.

phase_fit.note: Her protest frames femininity and domestic maturation as a threat to freedom and autonomy, which is the clearest match for Jo's early rebellious self-assertion.

phase_responses.gt_action: She gives her hair a tug and grumbles back, but keeps hold of the knitting instead of flinging the whole quarrel wider.
phase_responses.gt_speech: I hate the prim part of it; but I'll do my stint, all the same.
phase_responses.gt_thought: The words still chafe, yet she has learned that work can be a kind of strength. She resents the ladylike mold, but she is less bent on escaping duty than on proving she can bear it usefully.

voice.note: The action, complaint, and inward resolve fit Jo in chapter 12 well—still bristling at 'young lady' expectations, yet newly determined to prove her usefulness through duty—with no clear anachronism or knowledge beyond that point.

phase_fit.note: The thought centers on resenting feminine constraint yet deliberately treating duty and useful work as strength, which is the hallmark of agency redirected into family service rather than pure rebellion or later adult communion.

phase_responses.gt_action: She laughs shortly, lets the hair fall, and answers with blunt honesty rather than full rebellion.
phase_responses.gt_speech: I was never made for a fine young lady, and there's no use pretending it.
phase_responses.gt_thought: She no longer treats the moment as only a fight for liberty; it is also a question of truth. Better to own plainly what she is than perform a part to please others or to make a scene of herself.

voice.note: This sounds like Jo in chapter-27 range: the speech is plain, spirited, and period-appropriate, while the thought fits her maturing preference for honest self-knowledge over mere defiance without reaching beyond what she yet knows.

phase_fit.note: The key cue is the thought that frames her response as honest self-definition rather than sheer rebellion or dutiful compliance, which best fits the phase where Jo chooses truth over self-display as ambition and relationships become more complicated.

phase_responses.gt_action: She laughs and yields the point good-humoredly.
phase_responses.gt_speech: Very well, Meg; I’ll be as lady-like as I can, and no worse for the effort.
phase_responses.gt_thought: She no longer treats such correction as a threat to her selfhood, but as part of living easily with those she loves. What matters is not winning room for herself, but making herself fit kindly into the shared life of home.

voice.note: This fits chapter-41 Jo well: the speech is period-appropriate and lightly playful, and the yielding thought suits her matured willingness to bend for family peace without sounding anachronistic or beyond what she yet knows.

phase_fit.note: The thought frames accommodation not as reluctant duty or suppressed independence but as willingly fitting herself into a loving shared home, which most strongly matches Jo's chosen interdependence.

previous_attempt.gt_action: She smooths her loosened hair after a small protest and turns the sting into affectionate play instead of open defiance.
previous_attempt.gt_speech: Well, I shall never be very prim, Meg; but I can try not to plague you with my boyish ways.
previous_attempt.gt_thought: She still feels the old pinch at being pressed into a narrow feminine shape, but she weighs the bond before the victory. Keeping warmth with her sisters matters more than winning this skirmish over her independence.

voice.note: This fits chapter-41 Jo well: the speech keeps her old spirited resistance while yielding kindly, and the thought plausibly reflects her more mature habit of choosing sisterly harmony over a needless contest without using anachronistic language or later knowledge.

phase_fit.note: The response shows Jo still resisting feminine constraint inwardly, but deliberately redirecting herself toward preserving family warmth and not burdening her sisters, which fits agency disciplined by duty more than outright rebellion or later adult communion.

anchor_source.event_description: Jo is deeply frustrated by being a girl, missing her father, and being left at home while he is away at war. She openly resists the expectation that she should become a prim young lady, insisting she would rather keep her boyish ways and do active, masculine work.

anchor_source.key_moment: Christmas wish to be a boy
anchor_source.verbatim_passage:
"Really, girls, you are both to be blamed," said Meg, beginning to
lecture in her elder-sisterly fashion. "You are old enough to leave off
boyish tricks, and to behave better, Josephine. It didn't matter so much
when you were a little girl; but now you are so tall, and turn up your
hair, you should remember that you are a young lady."

"I'm not! and if turning up my hair makes me one, I'll wear it in two
tails till I'm twenty," cried Jo, pulling off her net, and shaking down
a chestnut mane. "I hate to think I've got to grow up, and be Miss
March, and wear long gowns, and look as prim as a China-aster! It's bad
enough to be a girl, anyway, when I like boys' games and work and
manners! I can't get over my disappointment in not being a boy; and it's
worse than ever now, for I'm dying to go and fight with papa, and I can
only stay at home and knit, like a poky old woman!" And Jo shook the
blue army-sock till the needles rattled like castanets, and her ball
bounded across the room.

"Poor Jo! It's too bad, but it can't be helped; so you must try to be
contented with making your name boyish, and playing brother to us
girls," said Beth, stroking the rough head at her knee with a hand that
all the dish-washing and dusting in the world could not make ungentle in
its touch.

"As for you, Amy," continued Meg, "you are altogether too particular and
prim. Your airs are funny now; but you'll grow up an affected little
goose, if you don't take care. I like your nice manners and refined ways
of speaking, when you don't try to be elegant; but your absurd words are
as bad as Jo's slang."

"If Jo is a tom-boy and Amy a goose, what am I, please?" asked Beth,
ready to share the lecture.

"You're a dear, and nothing else," answered Meg warmly; and no one
contradicted her, for the "Mouse" was the pet of the family.

anchor.note: The scenario matches the sisters-at-home lecture scene, Jo’s action and quoted speech accurately reflect her pulling off the net, shaking down her hair, and angrily shaking the blue army-sock, and the thought is directly supported by her complaint that growing up into a ‘young lady’ means losing the boyish freedom and active life she longs for.

discrimination.note: All adjacent pairs are meaningfully differentiated on the autonomy-versus-shared-duty axis: P0→P1 shifts from outright resistance to grudging duty, P1→P2 from dutiful compliance to truth-centered self-definition that resists relational molding, and P2→P3 from guarded self-direction to willing accommodation for shared home life.

probes.scenario: On a bright afternoon, Jo has leave to go out on an errand of her own when she learns that a poor neighbor's little children have been left alone in a cold room, and Marmee is delayed from home. No one asks her, but the house plainly needs quick hands.
probes.question: How does Josephine March respond when her own plan is crossed by this need close at hand?

phase_responses.gt_action: She lingers in the doorway, then turns toward the neighbor's house with a vexed shrug.
phase_responses.gt_speech: Well, I can't enjoy myself knowing it.
phase_responses.gt_thought: It feels provoking to have her liberty snatched up by another domestic claim. Still, she likes being stout-hearted and useful in a scrape, if she may do it in her own way.

voice.note: This fits early Jo well: she resents the interruption to her liberty, yet turns her energy toward helping in a brisk, self-willed way, and the diction is broadly period-appropriate aside from a slightly modern neatness in 'domestic claim.'

phase_fit.note: She is still irritated by the loss of freedom, but she voluntarily redirects her will into immediate practical service and values being 'useful,' which is most characteristic of agency disciplined by duty.

phase_responses.gt_action: She goes to the neighbor's house and sets about making the children warm and orderly.
phase_responses.gt_speech: Come, dears, we'll mend this as we can till help comes.
phase_responses.gt_thought: A need like this is work to be taken up, not fretted over. She has learned that strength is best proved by bearing family-like burdens cheerfully and making herself of use.

voice.note: This fits Jo in chapter 12: the brisk, practical action and plain, kindly speech suit her growing habit of turning strong will into usefulness, and nothing in the wording feels anachronistic or beyond what she knows.

phase_fit.note: The thought frames usefulness and cheerful burden-bearing as the right expression of her strength, which matches Jo's independence being redirected into practical service and family-like duty.

phase_responses.gt_action: She sends word postponing her errand, then stays with the children and manages the room.
phase_responses.gt_speech: My business can wait; this is the truer one today.
phase_responses.gt_thought: She measures the loss of her own hour against what is plainly wanted and feels the old tug of self-direction. Yet she distrusts selfish ambition when tenderness is being asked of her, and chooses the honest duty before her.

voice.note: This fits Jo at chapter 27: she would briskly sacrifice her own plan to be useful, and while phrases like 'the truer one' and 'selfish ambition' are a touch polished, they remain plausible in Alcott’s moral register and do not overstep her knowledge or era.

phase_fit.note: She explicitly redirects her own freedom into immediate practical service, framing the sacrificed personal errand as secondary to the concrete duty of caring for vulnerable children.

phase_responses.gt_action: She settles in the room and falls to tending the children as if it were the most natural errand in the world.
phase_responses.gt_speech: There, my dears; we shall be cosy presently.
phase_responses.gt_thought: Her own plan slips out of mind when she sees what is wanted. Such small homely needs draw her now, and she is happiest when her hands can make things easier for someone.

voice.note: This fits Jo after Beth’s death and before chapter 41’s end: the ready turn from personal liberty to useful, affectionate service feels true to her chosen domestic vocation, and the diction is period-appropriate and natural.

phase_fit.note: The thought that her own plan simply falls away and that she is happiest meeting small homely needs expresses agency fully integrated into caregiving and reciprocal domestic service, which best fits chosen communion.

previous_attempt.gt_action: She settles in the room, tends the children, and begins ordering things as if she belonged to the work.
previous_attempt.gt_speech: We'll make a comfortable time of it together.
previous_attempt.gt_thought: She no longer reads such interruption as theft from her freedom, but as a call into shared life. Care is not a chain now; it is a place where her energy naturally goes and does good.

voice.note: The action fits late-phase Jo, but the thought is too abstract and modern in its self-analysis—phrases like 'theft from her freedom,' 'call into shared life,' and 'Care is not a chain' sound like critical summary rather than Jo's chapter-41 inward language.

phase_fit.note: The thought explicitly frames care as a freely embraced form of shared life rather than a duty that interrupts autonomy, which most strongly matches Jo's integrated, reciprocal agency in chosen communion.

world.note: The scenario fits the domestic, realistic world of early Little Women, uses only characters and circumstances plausible by chapter 3, and echoes Jo’s charitable household sphere without reproducing a specific canonical scene.

weak_pairs.note: Both choose to forgo the personal errand and help immediately; the main difference is that Phase 0 still feels vexed while Phase 1 frames usefulness more cheerfully as duty, which is only a modest shift on this decision axis.

Both responses clearly subordinate Jo's own plans to nearby care work, with Phase 2 adding more reflective language about ambition and honesty but not changing the practical choice toward greater autonomy.

Both phases answer by embracing the needy relationship over personal freedom, and the difference is chiefly in ease and warmth of inward construal rather than a distinct decision on whether to bind herself through care.

discrimination.note: All adjacent pairs converge on the same overt choice—Jo gives up her own errand to care for the children—so the phase signal appears mostly as tonal/cognitive shading rather than clearly separated decisions on the autonomy-versus-shared-duty variable.

probes.scenario: At first light, Josephine March has her bundle packed for a day's walk to the next village, where a peddler will buy her pages and a teamster will take on helpers for the harvest road. Before she steps off, a younger sister comes in flushed and shivering, and her mother asks for steady hands at home.
probes.question: How does Josephine March answer that call at the doorway?

phase_responses.gt_action: Josephine sets down her bundle with a sharp face, but stays by the hearth and takes up the water kettle.
phase_responses.gt_speech: I can do it, only don't expect me to like it.
phase_responses.gt_thought: It feels like being tethered just as the gate was open. Home claims her because she is there, and she resents being made useful when she meant to choose her own day.

voice.note: The response fits early Jo's rebellious, useful-against-her-will temper and uses era-plausible language, with only a slightly polished thought but nothing knowledge-breaking or out of character.

phase_fit.note: Though she complies in action, her thought frames family need chiefly as an unwanted tether on her freedom, which matches Jo's early self-assertive resistance to domestic claims more than duty willingly embraced.

phase_responses.gt_action: Josephine unpacks her bundle and turns to the sickbed, setting her day aside to tend the room.
phase_responses.gt_speech: Send word to the peddler without me; she needs me here.
phase_responses.gt_thought: She still hates yielding her plans, but work done for her own people has begun to seem a sturdier sort of strength than roaming off for her own pleasure. If she can bear the burden, she ought to bear it.

voice.note: This fits Jo in chapter 12: she would chafe at losing her own plan yet turn her will toward family duty, and the diction is era-appropriate and plausible for an adolescent, if a touch polished in the thought.

phase_fit.note: The thought explicitly frames giving up her own plans as duty-bound family service and sees usefulness to her own people as a stronger form of strength, which is the hallmark of agency redirected into practical care.

phase_responses.gt_action: Josephine stands a moment with the bundle in hand, then hangs it back on the peg and sits beside her sister.
phase_responses.gt_speech: I'll stay today. The road can wait till another market.
phase_responses.gt_thought: She knows too well that chances pass and money is hard won, yet illness and parting have taught her how little command she truly has. Better to be plain and faithful than chase her own scheme while fearing what may be lost at home.

voice.note: This fits Jo in phase 2: the choice to forgo her own errand for family need, the plain speech, and the reflective thought about lost chances and limited control all sound plausible after her early adult disappointments without reaching beyond chapter 27 or using anachronistic language.

phase_fit.note: The decisive cue is her thought that illness and parting have taught her the limits of control, framing her choice of staying not just as duty but as a loss-tempered, honest renunciation of personal schemes.

phase_responses.gt_action: Josephine carries her bundle to the chest, puts it away, and begins ordering the day's care with calm hands.
phase_responses.gt_speech: We'll keep her warm, brew willow bark, and send for what is needed later.
phase_responses.gt_thought: The broken plan stings, but not as an injury to her freedom. Her will now goes readily into sheltering others, and shared duty feels less like a chain than the very shape of a good life.

voice.note: Jo's choice to put aside her own errand for family care fits phase-3's willing domestic devotion, and the language is broadly period-appropriate, though the thought is a touch abstractly summarized rather than distinctly Jo-like.

phase_fit.note: The thought explicitly frames shared duty as willingly embraced and constitutive of a good life, which best matches Jo's mature integration of agency into reciprocal care.

world.note: The scenario and all phase summaries fit a generic pre-industrial agrarian setting with no source-world leakage, keep Josephine March as protagonist, and present her at the required adolescent-to-young-adult life stages across phases.

weak_pairs.note: Both phases ultimately forgo the walk and choose caregiving over personal opportunity, with the main shift occurring in thought-level framing—from duty/usefulness to loss-limited faithfulness—rather than in a clearly different decision on the autonomy-versus-shared-duty axis.

Both responses answer the doorway call by staying, setting aside ambition, and orienting themselves to care, while Phase 3 mainly deepens the ease and positive valuation of shared duty rather than changing the decision itself.

discrimination.note: P0→P1 is separated because Phase 0 complies resentfully as an imposed tether, whereas Phase 1 more voluntarily redirects her agency into family service; the later adjacent pairs overlap in action and core choice, with differentiation carried mostly by cognitive style.

probes.scenario: Late at night, after Mrs. March sends the girls to bed in a quiet, anxious house, Meg lies awake beside Jo and hears a stifled sob in the dark. She touches Jo's wet cheek and asks what is wrong.
probes.question: How does Josephine March answer Meg and take in her own distress in that moment?

phase_responses.gt_action: She blurts out that she can't bear being a girl, then turns her face into the pillow as if to hide both tears and shame.
phase_responses.gt_speech: I can't get over my disappointment in not being a boy.
phase_responses.gt_thought: Her distress fixes on the indignity of being confined to girlhood and its helplessness. She is ashamed of crying because it feels like surrendering the hard, self-mastering freedom she wants.

voice.note: This matches Jo exactly in the early chapters: the line is near-textual to chapter 1, and the action, shame at tears, and resentment of girlhood all fit her adolescent, rebellious voice without anachronism or later knowledge.

phase_fit.note: The response centers on Jo's early rebellion against the constraints of girlhood and her wish to preserve hard, self-mastering autonomy rather than redirecting herself toward duty, loss-shaped honesty, or chosen mutual care.

previous_attempt.gt_action: She blurts out the loss of her hair with angry shame, then turns her face into the pillow as if to hide both tears and vanity.
previous_attempt.gt_speech: My hair! Oh, Meg, I can't help minding it.
previous_attempt.gt_thought: It feels unfair that duty should cost her the one bit of beauty she could claim. She is vexed less at crying than at being made weak and girlish by the loss.

voice.note: This wrongly imports a later event Jo cannot know by chapter 3—the loss of her hair—though the tone and phrasing otherwise fit her early shame at feminine vanity and resistance to weakness.

phase_fit.note: The response frames a personal sacrifice made for family duty—she resents the cost to her pride and femininity, but her agency is already being redirected into concrete service rather than pure rebellion or later adult communion.

phase_responses.gt_action: She lies still, then confesses through tears that she is crying for her hair, and tries to make light of it as a private weakness.
phase_responses.gt_speech: My--my hair!
phase_responses.gt_thought: She truly does not repent selling it; the pain is in finding vanity still alive in her after she meant to be brave and useful. She scolds herself for selfishness even while mourning her one beauty.

voice.note: This fits Jo at chapter 15 exactly: the brief, broken cry about her hair and the inward shame at grieving vanity while still standing by the sacrifice are period-appropriate, character-specific, and tonally right for her dutiful but still impetuous adolescence.

phase_fit.note: The response frames Jo's will as already committed to usefulness and family need—she does not regret the sacrifice itself, only her lingering vanity—matching independence disciplined into duty rather than autonomy-defending self-assertion or later loss-shaped adulthood.

phase_responses.gt_action: She gives a short, embarrassed confession about her hair, then checks herself and turns the talk away from her own feelings.
phase_responses.gt_speech: It's only my hair; don't mind me.
phase_responses.gt_thought: She knows private hurts can swell into theater if indulged, and she mistrusts making herself the heroine of the scene. The loss stings, but she would rather master it than let sorrow for herself burden Meg.

voice.note: This fits Jo well around chapter 27: the plain, brusque speech, embarrassed self-command, and wish not to make a fuss over her own hurt are true to her, with no anachronism or knowledge beyond the phase.

phase_fit.note: The response shows Jo actively disciplining her strong will into self-mastery so her private pain does not burden Meg, which fits independence redirected into practical family duty more than rebellious autonomy or later grief-shaped communion.

phase_responses.gt_action: She answers gently, owning the hurt without hiding from Meg's touch.
phase_responses.gt_speech: My hair.
phase_responses.gt_thought: The loss still pricks her pride, but she can bear being known in it instead of covering it with a joke or abruptness. Meg's touch makes the feeling less like a private humiliation than something tender she can share.

voice.note: The scene belongs to much earlier Jo, and at chapter 41 she would not plausibly frame the old hair-cutting hurt in such mature, self-aware language about being 'known' and sharing 'private humiliation,' which sounds too modern and phase-misaligned.

phase_fit.note: The response centers on accepting personal sacrifice in the context of family need and letting vulnerability be shared, which fits Jo's independence being redirected into duty rather than defended as pure autonomy.

previous_attempt.gt_action: She admits the hurt softly, then settles herself and tries to ease Meg instead of dwelling on her own sacrifice.
previous_attempt.gt_speech: I did mind it a little, but never mind me, dear.
previous_attempt.gt_thought: The tears are real, yet she does not treat them as shameful proof of vanity so much as one small cost of loving service. Her mind moves from self-reproach toward keeping the bedside gentle and companionable for Meg.

voice.note: The line fits Jo, but the thought is too phase-late and retrospective for chapter 41, framing her pain as maturely accepted 'loving service' rather than the more immediate, self-reproachful tenderness Jo shows in that earlier bedside scene.

phase_fit.note: The response frames personal hurt as an acceptable cost of loving service and redirects Jo's strong will toward comforting Meg, which best matches agency disciplined by family duty.

anchor_source.last_words: of living in her castle in the air.

anchor_source.verbatim_passage:
No one wanted to go to bed, when, at ten o'clock, Mrs. March put by the
last finished job, and said, "Come, girls." Beth went to the piano and
played the father's favorite hymn; all began bravely, but broke down
one by one, till Beth was left alone, singing with all her heart, for to
her music was always a sweet consoler.

"Go to bed and don't talk, for we must be up early, and shall need all
the sleep we can get. Good-night, my darlings," said Mrs. March, as the
hymn ended, for no one cared to try another.

They kissed her quietly, and went to bed as silently as if the dear
invalid lay in the next room. Beth and Amy soon fell asleep in spite of
the great trouble, but Meg lay awake, thinking the most serious thoughts
she had ever known in her short life. Jo lay motionless, and her sister
fancied that she was asleep, till a stifled sob made her exclaim, as she
touched a wet cheek,--

"Jo, dear, what is it? Are you crying about father?"

"No, not now."

"What then?"

"My--my hair!" burst out poor Jo, trying vainly to smother her emotion
in the pillow.

It did not sound at all comical to Meg, who kissed and caressed the
afflicted heroine in the tenderest manner.

"I'm not sorry," protested Jo, with a choke. "I'd do it again to-morrow,
if I could. It's only the vain, selfish part of me that goes and cries
in this silly way. Don't tell any one, it's all over now. I thought you
were asleep, so I just made a little private moan for my one beauty. How
came you to be awake?"

"I can't sleep, I'm so anxious," said Meg.

"Think about something pleasant, and you'll soon drop off."

"I tried it, but felt wider awake than ever."

"What did you think of?"

"Handsome faces,--eyes particularly," answered Meg, smiling to herself,
in the dark.

"What color do you like best?"

"Brown--that is, sometimes; blue are lovely."

Jo laughed, and Meg sharply ordered her not to talk, then amiably
promised to make her hair curl, and fell asleep to dream of living in
her castle in the air.

anchor.note: The scenario matches the bedside exchange after Mrs. March sends them to bed, and Jo’s response is faithful: she bursts out 'My--my hair!', admits it is the vain, selfish part of her grieving her 'one beauty,' and insists she is not sorry she sold it.

weak_pairs.note: Both responses subordinate Jo's private hurt to self-mastery and not burdening others, with phase 2 only slightly intensifying the anti-self-indulgent framing rather than shifting the autonomy-vs-shared-duty answer.

discrimination.note: P0→P1 is separated because Jo moves from distress centered on thwarted personal freedom to distress judged against usefulness and family service, and P2→P3 is separated because she shifts from guarding her feelings to allowing reciprocal comfort and shared tenderness.

probes.scenario: On a bright winter afternoon, Jo has leave to go out for her own pleasure, when a neighbor sends over in distress: her little girls are fretful, the maid has not come, and she begs one of the March girls to sit with them an hour. The lane beyond the house is full of snow and boys calling for a game, and no one has yet answered the message.
probes.question: How does Josephine March meet the call that comes just as her own hour opens before her?

phase_responses.gt_action: Jo lingers, then sends Amy in her stead if she can, keeping her cap in hand and edging toward the door.
phase_responses.gt_speech: Do be a good child, Amy; they'll only want a story and a patting.
phase_responses.gt_thought: It feels like a shabby trick that her one bit of liberty should be snatched for nursery work. If someone must go, she would rather dodge the harness than put her own neck in it.

voice.note: This fits early Jo well: she resents being pulled from her own liberty into feminine caretaking, tries to shift the duty onto Amy, and the speech and thought use period-plausible, spirited language without later-phase knowledge.

phase_fit.note: Her thought frames the request as an unfair theft of personal liberty and explicitly tries to evade domestic caregiving, which most strongly matches Jo's early rebellious self-assertion.

phase_responses.gt_action: Jo takes off her outdoor things and goes to the neighbor's house to mind the children for the hour.
phase_responses.gt_speech: Tell Marmee I shall be back soon; poor souls, they can't help being troublesome.
phase_responses.gt_thought: She hates losing her outing, but need looks different to her now. Being useful is work fit for strong hands too, and she can bear the disappointment if it lightens another woman's load.

voice.note: This fits Jo in chapter-12 range: she would grumble inwardly at losing her fun yet choose usefulness, and the speech and thought use era-appropriate, character-plausible language without later knowledge or modern phrasing.

phase_fit.note: The key cue is that Jo consciously gives up personal pleasure to meet an immediate family-like need and explicitly reframes usefulness and service as a worthy expression of her strength.

phase_responses.gt_action: Jo sends word that she will come for a shorter while, then sits with the children, carrying her notebook unopened in her pocket.
phase_responses.gt_speech: I'll do what I can till someone better comes; only don't expect me for the whole afternoon.

anchor_source.event_description: Jo wins the hundred-dollar prize for her sensational story and is overwhelmed by the letter and check, crying from the joy of being encouraged as a writer.
anchor_source.first_words: She said nothing of her plan
anchor_source.last_words: Hurrah for Dr. Jo, who always cures her patients!
anchor_source.verbatim_passage:
She said nothing of her plan at home, but fell to work next day, much to
the disquiet of her mother, who always looked a little anxious when
"genius took to burning." Jo had never tried this style before,
contenting herself with very mild romances for the "Spread Eagle." Her
theatrical experience and miscellaneous reading were of service now, for
they gave her some idea of dramatic effect, and supplied plot, language,
and costumes. Her story was as full of desperation and despair as her
limited acquaintance with those uncomfortable emotions enabled her to
make it, and, having located it in Lisbon, she wound up with an
earthquake, as a striking and appropriate _dénouement_. The manuscript
was privately despatched, accompanied by a note, modestly saying that if
the tale didn't get the prize, which the writer hardly dared expect, she
would be very glad to receive any sum it might be considered worth.

Six weeks is a long time to wait, and a still longer time for a girl to
keep a secret; but Jo did both, and was just beginning to give up all
hope of ever seeing her manuscript again, when a letter arrived which
almost took her breath away; for on opening it, a check for a hundred
dollars fell into her lap. For a minute she stared at it as if it had
been a snake, then she read her letter and began to cry. If the amiable
gentleman who wrote that kindly note could have known what intense
happiness he was giving a fellow-creature, I think he would devote his
leisure hours, if he has any, to that amusement; for Jo valued the
letter more than the money, because it was encouraging; and after years
of effort it was _so_ pleasant to find that she had learned to do
something, though it was only to write a sensation story.

            [Illustration: A check for one hundred dollars]

A prouder young woman was seldom seen than she, when, having composed
herself, she electrified the family by appearing before them with the
letter in one hand, the check in the other, announcing that she had won
the prize. Of course there was a great jubilee, and when the story came
every one read and praised it; though after her father had told her that
the language was good, the romance fresh and hearty, and the tragedy
quite thrilling, he shook his head, and said in his unworldly way,--

"You can do better than this, Jo. Aim at the highest, and never mind the
money."

"_I_ think the money is the best part of it. What _will_ you do with
such a fortune?" asked Amy, regarding the magic slip of paper with a
reverential eye.

"Send Beth and mother to the seaside for a month or two," answered Jo
promptly.

"Oh, how splendid! No, I can't do it, dear, it would be so selfish,"
cried Beth, who had clapped her thin hands, and taken a long breath, as
if pining for fresh ocean-breezes; then stopped herself, and motioned
away the check which her sister waved before her.

"Ah, but you shall go, I've set my heart on it; that's what I tried for,
and that's why I succeeded. I never get on when I think of myself alone,
so it will help me to work for you, don't you see? Besides, Marmee needs
the change, and she won't leave you, so you _must_ go. Won't it be fun
to see you come home plump and rosy again? Hurrah for Dr. Jo, who always
cures her patients!"

anchor.note: The scenario accurately matches the home setting and family reveal after Jo’s secret wait, the action and quoted speech are taken directly from the passage, and the thought is supported by the text’s emphasis that the encouraging letter meant more than the money and that Jo immediately dedicates the prize to Beth and Marmee.

Both responses construe the winnings as something to share lovingly with close others, so the difference is mainly tone—urgent family good versus chosen affectionate giving—rather than a distinct decision-variable answer.

anchor_source.verbatim_passage:
Blurred and blotted, faulty and feeble, as the lines were, they brought
a look of inexpressible comfort to Beth's face, for her one regret had
been that she had done so little; and this seemed to assure her that her
life had not been useless, that her death would not bring the despair
she feared. As she sat with the paper folded between her hands, the
charred log fell asunder. Jo started up, revived the blaze, and crept to
the bedside, hoping Beth slept.

"Not asleep, but so happy, dear. See, I found this and read it; I knew
you wouldn't care. Have I been all that to you, Jo?" she asked, with
wistful, humble earnestness.

"O Beth, so much, so much!" and Jo's head went down upon the pillow,
beside her sister's.

"Then I don't feel as if I'd wasted my life. I'm not so good as you make
me, but I _have_ tried to do right; and now, when it's too late to
begin even to do better, it's such a comfort to know that some one loves
me so much, and feels as if I'd helped them."

"More than any one in the world, Beth. I used to think I couldn't let
you go; but I'm learning to feel that I don't lose you; that you'll be
more to me than ever, and death can't part us, though it seems to."

"I know it cannot, and I don't fear it any longer, for I'm sure I shall
be your Beth still, to love and help you more than ever. You must take
my place, Jo, and be everything to father and mother when I'm gone. They
will turn to you, don't fail them; and if it's hard to work alone,
remember that I don't forget you, and that you'll be happier in doing
that than writing splendid books or seeing all the world; for love is
the only thing that we can carry with us when we go, and it makes the
end so easy."

"I'll try, Beth;" and then and there Jo renounced her old ambition,
pledged herself to a new and better one, acknowledging the poverty of
other desires, and feeling the blessed solace of a belief in the
immortality of love.

So the spring days came and went, the sky grew clearer, the earth
greener, the flowers were up fair and early, and the birds came back in
time to say good-by to Beth, who, like a tired but trustful child,
clung to the hands that had led her all her life, as father and mother
guided her tenderly through the Valley of the Shadow, and gave her up to God.

Seldom, except in books, do the dying utter memorable words, see
visions, or depart with beatified countenances; and those who have sped
many parting souls know that to most the end comes as naturally and
simply as sleep. As Beth had hoped, the "tide went out easily;" and in
the dark hour before the dawn, on the bosom where she had drawn her
first breath, she quietly drew her last, with no farewell but one loving
look, one little sigh.

anchor_source.verbatim_passage:
I suspect that the real attraction was a large library of fine books,
which was left to dust and spiders since Uncle March died. Jo remembered
the kind old gentleman, who used to let her build railroads and bridges
with his big dictionaries, tell her stories about the queer pictures in
his Latin books, and buy her cards of gingerbread whenever he met her in
the street. The dim, dusty room, with the busts staring down from the
tall book-cases, the cosy chairs, the globes, and, best of all, the
wilderness of books, in which she could wander where she liked, made the
library a region of bliss to her. The moment Aunt March took her nap, or
was busy with company, Jo hurried to this quiet place, and, curling
herself up in the easy-chair, devoured poetry, romance, history,
travels, and pictures, like a regular book-worm. But, like all
happiness, it did not last long; for as sure as she had just reached the
heart of the story, the sweetest verse of the song, or the most perilous
adventure of her traveller, a shrill voice called, "Josy-phine!
Josy-phine!" and she had to leave her paradise to wind yarn, wash the
poodle, or read Belsham's Essays by the hour together.

          [Illustration: Curling herself up in the big chair]

Jo's ambition was to do something very splendid; what it was she had no
idea, as yet, but left it for time to tell her; and, meanwhile, found
her greatest affliction in the fact that she couldn't read, run, and
ride as much as she liked. A quick temper, sharp tongue, and restless
spirit were always getting her into scrapes, and her life was a series
of ups and downs, which were both comic and pathetic. But the training
she received at Aunt March's was just what she needed; and the thought
that she was doing something to support herself made her happy, in spite
of the perpetual "Josy-phine!"

anchor_source.event_description: Jo wins the hundred-dollar prize for her sensational story and is overwhelmed by the letter and check, crying from the joy of being encouraged as a writer.
anchor_source.first_words: She said nothing of her plan
anchor_source.last_words: Hurrah for Dr. Jo, who always cures
anchor_source.verbatim_passage:
She said nothing of her plan at home, but fell to work next day, much to
the disquiet of her mother, who always looked a little anxious when
"genius took to burning." Jo had never tried this style before,
contenting herself with very mild romances for the "Spread Eagle." Her
theatrical experience and miscellaneous reading were of service now, for
they gave her some idea of dramatic effect, and supplied plot, language,
and costumes. Her story was as full of desperation and despair as her
limited acquaintance with those uncomfortable emotions enabled her to
make it, and, having located it in Lisbon, she wound up with an
earthquake, as a striking and appropriate _dénouement_. The manuscript
was privately despatched, accompanied by a note, modestly saying that if
the tale didn't get the prize, which the writer hardly dared expect, she
would be very glad to receive any sum it might be considered worth.

Six weeks is a long time to wait, and a still longer time for a girl to
keep a secret; but Jo did both, and was just beginning to give up all
hope of ever seeing her manuscript again, when a letter arrived which
almost took her breath away; for on opening it, a check for a hundred
dollars fell into her lap. For a minute she stared at it as if it had
been a snake, then she read her letter and began to cry. If the amiable
gentleman who wrote that kindly note could have known what intense
happiness he was giving a fellow-creature, I think he would devote his
leisure hours, if he has any, to that amusement; for Jo valued the
letter more than the money, because it was encouraging; and after years
of effort it was _so_ pleasant to find that she had learned to do
something, though it was only to write a sensation story.

            [Illustration: A check for one hundred dollars]

A prouder young woman was seldom seen than she, when, having composed
herself, she electrified the family by appearing before them with the
letter in one hand, the check in the other, announcing that she had won
the prize. Of course there was a great jubilee, and when the story came
every one read and praised it; though after her father had told her that
the language was good, the romance fresh and hearty, and the tragedy
quite thrilling, he shook his head, and said in his unworldly way,--

"You can do better than this, Jo. Aim at the highest, and never mind the
money."

"_I_ think the money is the best part of it. What _will_ you do with
such a fortune?" asked Amy, regarding the magic slip of paper with a
reverential eye.

"Send Beth and mother to the seaside for a month or two," answered Jo
promptly.

"Oh, how splendid! No, I can't do it, dear, it would be so selfish,"
cried Beth, who had clapped her thin hands, and taken a long breath, as
if pining for fresh ocean-breezes; then stopped herself, and motioned
away the check which her sister waved before her.

"Ah, but you shall go, I've set my heart on it; that's what I tried for,
and that's why I succeeded. I never get on when I think of myself alone,
so it will help me to work for you, don't you see? Besides, Marmee needs
the change, and she won't leave you, so you _must_ go. Won't it be fun
to see you come home plump and rosy again? Hurrah for Dr. Jo, who always
cures her patients!"

anchor_source.event_description: Jo spends Beth's final illness constantly at her bedside, nursing her through pain and decline, and is deeply affected by Beth's quiet courage and self-forgetting goodness.

anchor_source.last_words: but one loving look, one little sigh.
anchor_source.verbatim_passage:
Jo never left her for an hour since Beth had said, "I feel stronger when you are here." She slept on a couch in the room, waking often to renew the fire, to feed, lift, or wait upon the patient creature who seldom asked for anything, and "tried not to be a trouble." All day she haunted the room, jealous of any other nurse, and prouder of being chosen then than of any honor her life ever brought her. Precious and helpful hours to Jo, for now her heart received the teaching that it needed; lessons in patience were so sweetly taught her that she could not fail to learn them; charity for all, the lovely spirit that can forgive and truly forget unkindness, the loyalty to duty that makes the hardest easy, and the sincere faith that fears nothing, but trusts undoubtingly.

Often, when she woke, Jo found Beth reading in her well-worn little book, heard her singing softly, to beguile the sleepless night, or saw her lean her face upon her hands, while slow tears dropped through the transparent fingers; and Jo would lie watching her, with thoughts too deep for tears, feeling that Beth, in her simple, unselfish way, was trying to wean herself from the dear old life, and fit herself for the life to come, by sacred words of comfort, quiet prayers, and the music she loved so well.

Seeing this did more for Jo than the wisest sermons, the saintliest hymns, the most fervent prayers that any voice could utter; for, with eyes made clear by many tears, and a heart softened by the tenderest sorrow, she recognized the beauty of her sister's life,--uneventful, unambitious, yet full of the genuine virtues which "smell sweet, and blossom in the dust," the self-forgetfulness that makes the humblest on earth remembered soonest in heaven, the true success which is possible to all.

One night, when Beth looked among the books upon her table, to find something to make her forget the mortal weariness that was almost as hard to bear as pain, as she turned the leaves of her old favorite Pilgrim's Progress, she found a little paper, scribbled over in Jo's hand. The name caught her eye, and the blurred look of the lines made her sure that tears had fallen on it.

"Poor Jo! she's fast asleep, so I won't wake her to ask leave; she shows me all her things, and I don't think she'll mind if I look at this," thought Beth, with a glance at her sister, who lay on the rug, with the tongs beside her, ready to wake up the minute the log fell apart.


                               "MY BETH.

        "Sitting patient in the shadow
           Till the blessed light shall come,
         A serene and saintly presence
           Sanctifies our troubled home.
         Earthly joys and hopes and sorrows
           Break like ripples on the strand
         Of the deep and solemn river
           Where her willing feet now stand.

        "O my sister, passing from me,
           Out of human care and strife,
         Leave me, as a gift, those virtues
           Which have beautified your life.
         Dear, bequeath me that great patience
           Which has power to sustain
         A cheerful, uncomplaining spirit
           In its prison-house of pain.

        "Give me, for I need it sorely,
           Of that courage, wise and sweet,
         Which has made the path of duty
           Green beneath your willing feet.
         Give me that unselfish nature,
           That with charity divine
         Can pardon wrong for love's dear sake--
           Meek heart, forgive me mine!

        "Thus our parting daily loseth
          Something of its bitter pain,
         And while learning this hard lesson,
           My great loss becomes my gain.
         For the touch of grief will render
           My wild nature more serene,
         Give to life new aspirations,
           A new trust in the unseen.

        "Henceforth, safe across the river,
           I shall see forevermore
         A beloved, household spirit
           Waiting for me on the shore.
         Hope and faith, born of my sorrow,
           Guardian angels shall become,
         And the sister gone before me
           By their hands shall lead me home."

Blurred and blotted, faulty and feeble, as the lines were, they brought
a look of inexpressible comfort to Beth's face, for her one regret had
been that she had done so little; and this seemed to assure her that her
life had not been useless, that her death would not bring the despair
she feared. As she sat with the paper folded between her hands, the
charred log fell asunder. Jo started up, revived the blaze, and crept to
the bedside, hoping Beth slept.

"Not asleep, but so happy, dear. See, I found this and read it; I knew
you wouldn't care. Have I been all that to you, Jo?" she asked, with
wistful, humble earnestness.

"O Beth, so much, so much!" and Jo's head went down upon the pillow,
beside her sister's.

"Then I don't feel as if I'd wasted my life. I'm not so good as you make
me, but I _have_ tried to do right; and now, when it's too late to
begin even to do better, it's such a comfort to know that some one loves
me so much, and feels as if I'd helped them."

"More than any one in the world, Beth. I used to think I couldn't let
you go; but I'm learning to feel that I don't lose you; that you'll be
more to me than ever, and death can't part us, though it seems to."

"I know it cannot, and I don't fear it any longer, for I'm sure I shall
be your Beth still, to love and help you more than ever. You must take
my place, Jo, and be everything to father and mother when I'm gone. They
will turn to you, don't fail them; and if it's hard to work alone,
remember that I don't forget you, and that you'll be happier in doing
that than writing splendid books or seeing all the world; for love is
the only thing that we can carry with us when we go, and it makes the
end so easy."

"I'll try, Beth;" and then and there Jo renounced her old ambition,
pledged herself to a new and better one, acknowledging the poverty of
other desires, and feeling the blessed solace of a belief in the
immortality of love.

So the spring days came and went, the sky grew clearer, the earth
greener, the flowers were up fair and early, and the birds came back in
time to say good-by to Beth, who, like a tired but trustful child, clung
to the hands that had led her all her life, as father and mother guided
her tenderly through the Valley of the Shadow, and gave her up to God.

Seldom, except in books, do the dying utter memorable words, see
visions, or depart with beatified countenances; and those who have sped
many parting souls know that to most the end comes as naturally and
simply as sleep. As Beth had hoped, the "tide went out easily;" and in
the dark hour before the dawn, on the bosom where she had drawn her
first breath, she quietly drew her last, with no farewell but one loving
look, one little sigh.

anchor_source.verbatim_passage:
"I'm glad you _are_ poor; I couldn't bear a rich husband," said Jo
decidedly, adding, in a softer tone, "Don't fear poverty; I've known it
long enough to lose my dread, and be happy working for those I love; and
don't call yourself old,--forty is the prime of life. I couldn't help
loving you if you were seventy!"

The Professor found that so touching that he would have been glad of his
handkerchief, if he could have got at it; as he couldn't, Jo wiped his
eyes for him, and said, laughing, as she took away a bundle or two,--

"I may be strong-minded, but no one can say I'm out of my sphere now,
for woman's special mission is supposed to be drying tears and bearing
burdens. I'm to carry my share, Friedrich, and help to earn the home.
Make up your mind to that, or I'll never go," she added resolutely, as
he tried to reclaim his load.

"We shall see. Haf you patience to wait a long time, Jo? I must go away
and do my work alone. I must help my boys first, because, even for you,
I may not break my word to Minna. Can you forgif that, and be happy
while we hope and wait?"

"Yes, I know I can; for we love one another, and that makes all the rest
easy to bear. I have my duty, also, and my work. I couldn't enjoy myself
if I neglected them even for you, so there's no need of hurry or
impatience. You can do your part out West, I can do mine here, and both
be happy hoping for the best, and leaving the future to be as God
wills."

"Ah! thou gifest me such hope and courage, and I haf nothing to gif back
but a full heart and these empty hands," cried the Professor, quite
overcome.

                   [Illustration: Under the umbrella]

Jo never, never would learn to be proper; for when he said that as they
stood upon the steps, she just put both hands into his, whispering
tenderly, "Not empty now;" and, stooping down, kissed her Friedrich
under the umbrella. It was dreadful, but she would have done it if the
flock of draggle-tailed sparrows on the hedge had been human beings, for
she was very far gone indeed, and quite regardless of everything but her
own happiness. Though it came in such a very simple guise, that was the
crowning moment of both their lives, when, turning from the night and
storm and loneliness to the household light and warmth and peace waiting
to receive them, with a glad "Welcome home!" Jo led her lover in, and
shut the door.

anchor_source.verbatim_passage:
"Really, girls, you are both to be blamed," said Meg, beginning to
lecture in her elder-sisterly fashion. "You are old enough to leave off
boyish tricks, and to behave better, Josephine. It didn't matter so much
when you were a little girl; but now you are so tall, and turn up your
hair, you should remember that you are a young lady."

"I'm not! and if turning up my hair makes me one, I'll wear it in two
tails till I'm twenty," cried Jo, pulling off her net, and shaking down
a chestnut mane. "I hate to think I've got to grow up, and be Miss
March, and wear long gowns, and look as prim as a China-aster! It's bad
enough to be a girl, anyway, when I like boys' games and work and
manners! I can't get over my disappointment in not being a boy; and it's
worse than ever now, for I'm dying to go and fight with papa, and I can
only stay at home and knit, like a poky old woman!" And Jo shook the
blue army-sock till the needles rattled like castanets, and her ball
bounded across the room.

"Poor Jo! It's too bad, but it can't be helped; so you must try to be
contented with making your name boyish, and playing brother to us
girls," said Beth, stroking the rough head at her knee with a hand that
all the dish-washing and dusting in the world could not make ungentle in
its touch.

"As for you, Amy," continued Meg, "you are altogether too particular and
prim. Your airs are funny now; but you'll grow up an affected little
goose, if you don't take care. I like your nice manners and refined ways
of speaking, when you don't try to be elegant; but your absurd words are
as bad as Jo's slang."

"If Jo is a tom-boy and Amy a goose, what am I, please?" asked Beth,
ready to share the lecture.

"You're a dear, and nothing else," answered Meg warmly; and no one
contradicted her, for the "Mouse" was the pet of the family.

As young readers like to know "how people look," we will take this
moment to give them a little sketch of the four sisters, who sat
knitting away in the twilight, while the December snow fell quietly
without, and the fire crackled cheerfully within. It was a comfortable
old room, though the carpet was faded and the furniture very plain; for
a good picture or two hung on the walls, books filled the recesses,
chrysanthemums and Christmas roses bloomed in the windows, and a
pleasant atmosphere of home-peace pervaded it.

Margaret, the eldest of the four, was sixteen, and very pretty, being
plump and fair, with large eyes, plenty of soft, brown hair, a sweet
mouth, and white hands, of which she was rather vain. Fifteen-year-old
Jo was very tall, thin, and brown, and reminded one of a colt; for she
never seemed to know what to do with her long limbs, which were very
much in her way. She had a decided mouth, a comical nose, and sharp,
gray eyes, which appeared to see everything, and were by turns fierce,
funny, or thoughtful. Her long, thick hair was her one beauty; but it
was usually bundled into a net, to be out of her way. Round shoulders
had Jo, big hands and feet, a fly-away look to her clothes, and the
uncomfortable appearance of a girl who was rapidly shooting up into a
woman, and didn't like it.

anchor_source.verbatim_passage:
Frank, Beth, Amy, and Grace sat down to watch the game played by the
other eight. Mr. Brooke chose Meg, Kate, and Fred; Laurie took Sallie,
Jo, and Ned. The Englishers played well; but the Americans played
better, and contested every inch of the ground as strongly as if the
spirit of '76 inspired them. Jo and Fred had several skirmishes, and
once narrowly escaped high words. Jo was through the last wicket, and
had missed the stroke, which failure ruffled her a good deal. Fred was
close behind her, and his turn came before hers; he gave a stroke, his
ball hit the wicket, and stopped an inch on the wrong side. No one was
very near; and running up to examine, he gave it a sly nudge with his
toe, which put it just an inch on the right side.

"I'm through! Now, Miss Jo, I'll settle you, and get in first," cried
the young gentleman, swinging his mallet for another blow.

             [Illustration: Now, Miss Jo, I'll settle you]

"You pushed it; I saw you; it's my turn now," said Jo sharply.

"Upon my word, I didn't move it; it rolled a bit, perhaps, but that is
allowed; so stand off, please, and let me have a go at the stake."

"We don't cheat in America, but you can, if you choose," said Jo
angrily.

"Yankees are a deal the most tricky, everybody knows. There you go!"
returned Fred, croqueting her ball far away.

Jo opened her lips to say something rude, but checked herself in time,
colored up to her forehead, and stood a minute, hammering down a wicket
with all her might, while Fred hit the stake, and declared himself out
with much exultation. She went off to get her ball, and was a long time
finding it, among the bushes; but she came back, looking cool and quiet,
and waited her turn patiently. It took several strokes to regain the
place she had lost; and, when she got there, the other side had nearly
won, for Kate's ball was the last but one, and lay near the stake.

"By George, it's all up with us! Good-by, Kate. Miss Jo owes me one, so
you are finished," cried Fred excitedly, as they all drew near to see
the finish.

"Yankees have a trick of being generous to their enemies," said Jo, with
a look that made the lad redden, "especially when they beat them," she
added, as, leaving Kate's ball untouched, she won the game by a clever
stroke.

Laurie threw up his hat; then remembered that it wouldn't do to exult
over the defeat of his guests, and stopped in the middle of a cheer to
whisper to his friend,--

"Good for you, Jo! He did cheat, I saw him; we can't tell him so, but he
won't do it again, take my word for it."

Meg drew her aside, under pretence of pinning up a loose braid, and said
approvingly,--

"It was dreadfully provoking; but you kept your temper, and I'm so glad,
Jo."

"Don't praise me, Meg, for I could box his ears this minute. I should
certainly have boiled over if I hadn't stayed among the nettles till I
got my rage under enough to hold my tongue. It's simmering now, so I
hope he'll keep out of my way," returned Jo, biting her lips, as she
glowered at Fred from under her big hat.

anchor_source.verbatim_passage:
Well, it was printed, and she got three hundred dollars for it; likewise
plenty of praise and blame, both so much greater than she expected that
she was thrown into a state of bewilderment, from which it took her some
time to recover.

"You said, mother, that criticism would help me; but how can it, when
it's so contradictory that I don't know whether I've written a promising
book or broken all the ten commandments?" cried poor Jo, turning over a
heap of notices, the perusal of which filled her with pride and joy one
minute, wrath and dire dismay the next. "This man says 'An exquisite
book, full of truth, beauty, and earnestness; all is sweet, pure, and
healthy,'" continued the perplexed authoress. "The next, 'The theory of
the book is bad, full of morbid fancies, spiritualistic ideas, and
unnatural characters.' Now, as I had no theory of any kind, don't
believe in Spiritualism, and copied my characters from life, I don't see
how this critic _can_ be right. Another says, 'It's one of the best
American novels which has appeared for years' (I know better than that);
and the next asserts that 'though it is original, and written with great
force and feeling, it is a dangerous book.' 'Tisn't! Some make fun of
it, some over-praise, and nearly all insist that I had a deep theory to
expound, when I only wrote it for the pleasure and the money. I wish I'd
printed it whole or not at all, for I do hate to be so misjudged."

Her family and friends administered comfort and commendation liberally;
yet it was a hard time for sensitive, high-spirited Jo, who meant so
well, and had apparently done so ill. But it did her good, for those
whose opinion had real value gave her the criticism which is an author's
best education; and when the first soreness was over, she could laugh at
her poor little book, yet believe in it still, and feel herself the
wiser and stronger for the buffeting she had received.

"Not being a genius, like Keats, it won't kill me," she said stoutly;
"and I've got the joke on my side, after all; for the parts that were
taken straight out of real life are denounced as impossible and absurd,
and the scenes that I made up out of my own silly head are pronounced
'charmingly natural, tender, and true.' So I'll comfort myself with
that; and when I'm ready, I'll up again and take another."

anchor_source.verbatim_passage:
"Really, girls, you are both to be blamed," said Meg, beginning to
lecture in her elder-sisterly fashion. "You are old enough to leave off
boyish tricks, and to behave better, Josephine. It didn't matter so much
when you were a little girl; but now you are so tall, and turn up your
hair, you should remember that you are a young lady."

"I'm not! and if turning up my hair makes me one, I'll wear it in two
tails till I'm twenty," cried Jo, pulling off her net, and shaking down
a chestnut mane. "I hate to think I've got to grow up, and be Miss
March, and wear long gowns, and look as prim as a China-aster! It's bad
enough to be a girl, anyway, when I like boys' games and work and
manners! I can't get over my disappointment in not being a boy; and it's
worse than ever now, for I'm dying to go and fight with papa, and I can
only stay at home and knit, like a poky old woman!" And Jo shook the
blue army-sock till the needles rattled like castanets, and her ball
bounded across the room.

"Poor Jo! It's too bad, but it can't be helped; so you must try to be
contented with making your name boyish, and playing brother to us
girls," said Beth, stroking the rough head at her knee with a hand that
all the dish-washing and dusting in the world could not make ungentle in
its touch.

"As for you, Amy," continued Meg, "you are altogether too particular and
prim. Your airs are funny now; but you'll grow up an affected little
goose, if you don't take care. I like your nice manners and refined ways
of speaking, when you don't try to be elegant; but your absurd words are
as bad as Jo's slang."

anchor_source.event_description: When their mother leaves for Washington, Jo struggles to hold back tears, then regains herself by accepting the family rule to 'hope and keep busy.' She immediately throws herself back into ordinary duties and prepares to continue her work and correspondence.
anchor_source.first_words: "I feel as if there had
anchor_source.last_words: like a shorn sheep on a wintry day."
anchor_source.verbatim_passage:
"I feel as if there had been an earthquake," said Jo, as their neighbors
went home to breakfast, leaving them to rest and refresh themselves.

"It seems as if half the house was gone," added Meg forlornly.

Beth opened her lips to say something, but could only point to the pile
of nicely-mended hose which lay on mother's table, showing that even in
her last hurried moments she had thought and worked for them. It was a
little thing, but it went straight to their hearts; and, in spite of
their brave resolutions, they all broke down, and cried bitterly.

Hannah wisely allowed them to relieve their feelings, and, when the
shower showed signs of clearing up, she came to the rescue, armed with a
coffee-pot.

"Now, my dear young ladies, remember what your ma said, and don't fret.
Come and have a cup of coffee all round, and then let's fall to work,
and be a credit to the family."

Coffee was a treat, and Hannah showed great tact in making it that
morning. No one could resist her persuasive nods, or the fragrant
invitation issuing from the nose of the coffee-pot. They drew up to the
table, exchanged their handkerchiefs for napkins, and in ten minutes
were all right again.

"'Hope and keep busy;' that's the motto for us, so let's see who will
remember it best. I shall go to Aunt March, as usual. Oh, won't she
lecture though!" said Jo, as she sipped with returning spirit.

"I shall go to my Kings, though I'd much rather stay at home and attend
to things here," said Meg, wishing she hadn't made her eyes so red.

"No need of that; Beth and I can keep house perfectly well," put in Amy,
with an important air.

"Hannah will tell us what to do; and we'll have everything nice when you
come home," added Beth, getting out her mop and dish-tub without delay.

"I think anxiety is very interesting," observed Amy, eating sugar,
pensively.

The girls couldn't help laughing, and felt better for it, though Meg
shook her head at the young lady who could find consolation in a
sugar-bowl.

The sight of the turn-overs made Jo sober again; and when the two went
out to their daily tasks, they looked sorrowfully back at the window
where they were accustomed to see their mother's face. It was gone; but
Beth had remembered the little household ceremony, and there she was,
nodding away at them like a rosy-faced mandarin.

"That's so like my Beth!" said Jo, waving her hat, with a grateful face.
"Good-by, Meggy; I hope the Kings won't train to-day. Don't fret about
father, dear," she added, as they parted.

"And I hope Aunt March won't croak. Your hair _is_ becoming, and it
looks very boyish and nice," returned Meg, trying not to smile at the
curly head, which looked comically small on her tall sister's shoulders.

"That's my only comfort;" and, touching her hat _à la_ Laurie, away went
Jo, feeling like a shorn sheep on a wintry day.

anchor.note: The scenario fits the breakfast-after-Marmee-leaves scene, and Jo’s action and quoted speech closely match the text; the thought is a reasonable inference from the passage’s emphasis on hope, busyness, and her going off to Aunt March despite the sorrow.

anchor_source.event_description: Laurie confesses his love for Jo and asks her to marry him; Jo refuses him honestly, insisting she cannot make herself love him and that marriage would make them miserable.
anchor_source.first_words: Laurie was a young lover, but
anchor_source.last_words: the better for both of us,--so now!
anchor_source.verbatim_passage:
Laurie was a young lover, but he was in earnest, and meant to "have it
out," if he died in the attempt; so he plunged into the subject with
characteristic impetuosity, saying in a voice that _would_ get choky now
and then, in spite of manful efforts to keep it steady,--

"I've loved you ever since I've known you, Jo; couldn't help it, you've
been so good to me. I've tried to show it, but you wouldn't let me; now
I'm going to make you hear, and give me an answer, for I _can't_ go on
so any longer."

"I wanted to save you this; I thought you'd understand--" began Jo,
finding it a great deal harder than she expected.

"I know you did; but girls are so queer you never know what they mean.
They say No when they mean Yes, and drive a man out of his wits just for
the fun of it," returned Laurie, entrenching himself behind an
undeniable fact.

"_I_ don't. I never wanted to make you care for me so, and I went away
to keep you from it if I could."

"I thought so; it was like you, but it was no use. I only loved you all
the more, and I worked hard to please you, and I gave up billiards and
everything you didn't like, and waited and never complained, for I hoped
you'd love me, though I'm not half good enough--" here there was a choke
that couldn't be controlled, so he decapitated buttercups while he
cleared his "confounded throat."

"Yes, you are; you're a great deal too good for me, and I'm so grateful
to you, and so proud and fond of you, I don't see why I can't love you
as you want me to. I've tried, but I can't change the feeling, and it
would be a lie to say I do when I don't."

"Really, truly, Jo?"

He stopped short, and caught both her hands as he put his question with
a look that she did not soon forget.

"Really, truly, dear."

They were in the grove now, close by the stile; and when the last words
fell reluctantly from Jo's lips, Laurie dropped her hands and turned as
if to go on, but for once in his life that fence was too much for him;
so he just laid his head down on the mossy post, and stood so still that
Jo was frightened.

        [Illustration: He laid his head down on the mossy post]

"O Teddy, I'm so sorry, so desperately sorry, I could kill myself if it
would do any good! I wish you wouldn't take it so hard. I can't help it;
you know it's impossible for people to make themselves love other people
if they don't," cried Jo inelegantly but remorsefully, as she softly
patted his shoulder, remembering the time when he had comforted her so
long ago.

"They do sometimes," said a muffled voice from the post.

"I don't believe it's the right sort of love, and I'd rather not try
it," was the decided answer.

There was a long pause, while a blackbird sung blithely on the willow by
the river, and the tall grass rustled in the wind. Presently Jo said
very soberly, as she sat down on the step of the stile,--

"Laurie, I want to tell you something."

He started as if he had been shot, threw up his head, and cried out, in
a fierce tone--

"_Don't_ tell me that, Jo; I can't bear it now!"

"Tell what?" she asked, wondering at his violence.

"That you love that old man."

"What old man?" demanded Jo, thinking he must mean his grandfather.

"That devilish Professor you were always writing about. If you say you
love him, I know I shall do something desperate;" and he looked as if he
would keep his word, as he clenched his hands, with a wrathful spark in
his eyes.

Jo wanted to laugh, but restrained herself, and said warmly, for she,
too, was getting excited with all this,--

"Don't swear, Teddy! He isn't old, nor anything bad, but good and kind,
and the best friend I've got, next to you. Pray, don't fly into a
passion; I want to be kind, but I know I shall get angry if you abuse my
Professor. I haven't the least idea of loving him or anybody else."

"But you will after a while, and then what will become of me?"

"You'll love some one else too, like a sensible boy, and forget all this
trouble."

"I _can't_ love any one else; and I'll never forget you, Jo, never!
never!" with a stamp to emphasize his passionate words.

"What _shall_ I do with him?" sighed Jo, finding that emotions were more
unmanageable than she expected. "You haven't heard what I wanted to tell
you. Sit down and listen; for indeed I want to do right and make you
happy," she said, hoping to soothe him with a little reason, which
proved that she knew nothing about love.

Seeing a ray of hope in that last speech, Laurie threw himself down on
the grass at her feet, leaned his arm on the lower step of the stile,
and looked up at her with an expectant face. Now that arrangement was
not conducive to calm speech or clear thought on Jo's part; for how
_could_ she say hard things to her boy while he watched her with eyes
full of love and longing, and lashes still wet with the bitter drop or
two her hardness of heart had wrung from him? She gently turned his head
away, saying, as she stroked the wavy hair which had been allowed to
grow for her sake,--how touching that was, to be sure!--

"I agree with mother that you and I are not suited to each other,
because our quick tempers and strong wills would probably make us very
miserable, if we were so foolish as to--" Jo paused a little over the
last word, but Laurie uttered it with a rapturous expression,--

"Marry,--no, we shouldn't! If you loved me, Jo, I should be a perfect
saint, for you could make me anything you like."

"No, I can't. I've tried it and failed, and I won't risk our happiness
by such a serious experiment. We don't agree and we never shall; so
we'll be good friends all our lives, but we won't go and do anything
rash."

"Yes, we will if we get the chance," muttered Laurie rebelliously.

"Now do be reasonable, and take a sensible view of the case," implored
Jo, almost at her wit's end.

"I won't be reasonable; I don't want to take what you call 'a sensible
view;' it won't help me, and it only makes you harder. I don't believe
you've got any heart."

"I wish I hadn't!"

There was a little quiver in Jo's voice, and, thinking it a good omen,
Laurie turned round, bringing all his persuasive powers to bear as he
said, in the wheedlesome tone that had never been so dangerously
wheedlesome before,--

"Don't disappoint us, dear! Every one expects it. Grandpa has set his
heart upon it, your people like it, and I can't get on without you. Say
you will, and let's be happy. Do, do!"

Not until months afterward did Jo understand how she had the strength of
mind to hold fast to the resolution she had made when she decided that
she did not love her boy, and never could. It was very hard to do, but
she did it, knowing that delay was both useless and cruel.

"I can't say 'Yes' truly, so I won't say it at all. You'll see that I'm
right, by and by, and thank me for it"--she began solemnly.

"I'll be hanged if I do!" and Laurie bounced up off the grass, burning
with indignation at the bare idea.

"Yes, you will!" persisted Jo; "you'll get over this after a while, and
find some lovely, accomplished girl, who will adore you, and make a fine
mistress for your fine house. I shouldn't. I'm homely and awkward and
odd and old, and you'd be ashamed of me, and we should quarrel,--we
can't help it even now, you see,--and I shouldn't like elegant society
and you would, and you'd hate my scribbling, and I couldn't get on
without it, and we should be unhappy, and wish we hadn't done it, and
everything would be horrid!"

"Anything more?" asked Laurie, finding it hard to listen patiently to
this prophetic burst.

"Nothing more, except that I don't believe I shall ever marry. I'm happy
as I am, and love my liberty too well to be in any hurry to give it up
for any mortal man."

"I know better!" broke in Laurie. "You think so now; but there'll come a
time when you _will_ care for somebody, and you'll love him
tremendously, and live and die for him. I know you will, it's your way,
and I shall have to stand by and see it;" and the despairing lover cast
his hat upon the ground with a gesture that would have seemed comical,
if his face had not been so tragical.

"Yes, I _will_ live and die for him, if he ever comes and makes me love
him in spite of myself, and you must do the best you can!" cried Jo,
losing patience with poor Teddy. "I've done my best, but you _won't_ be
reasonable, and it's selfish of you to keep teasing for what I can't
give. I shall always be fond of you, very fond indeed, as a friend, but
I'll never marry you; and the sooner you believe it, the better for both
of us,--so now!"

anchor_source.verbatim_passage:
"Don't, Jo; it's so boyish!"

"That's why I do it."

"I detest rude, unlady-like girls!"

"I hate affected, niminy-piminy chits!"

"'Birds in their little nests agree,'" sang Beth, the peace-maker, with
such a funny face that both sharp voices softened to a laugh, and the
"pecking" ended for that time.

"Really, girls, you are both to be blamed," said Meg, beginning to
lecture in her elder-sisterly fashion. "You are old enough to leave off
boyish tricks, and to behave better, Josephine. It didn't matter so much
when you were a little girl; but now you are so tall, and turn up your
hair, you should remember that you are a young lady."

"I'm not! and if turning up my hair makes me one, I'll wear it in two
tails till I'm twenty," cried Jo, pulling off her net, and shaking down
a chestnut mane. "I hate to think I've got to grow up, and be Miss
March, and wear long gowns, and look as prim as a China-aster! It's bad
enough to be a girl, anyway, when I like boys' games and work and
manners! I can't get over my disappointment in not being a boy; and it's
worse than ever now, for I'm dying to go and fight with papa, and I can
only stay at home and knit, like a poky old woman!" And Jo shook the
blue army-sock till the needles rattled like castanets, and her ball
bounded across the room.

"Poor Jo! It's too bad, but it can't be helped; so you must try to be
contented with making your name boyish, and playing brother to us
girls," said Beth, stroking the rough head at her knee with a hand that
all the dish-washing and dusting in the world could not make ungentle in
its touch.

"As for you, Amy," continued Meg, "you are altogether too particular and
prim. Your airs are funny now; but you'll grow up an affected little
goose, if you don't take care. I like your nice manners and refined ways
of speaking, when you don't try to be elegant; but your absurd words are
as bad as Jo's slang."

"If Jo is a tom-boy and Amy a goose, what am I, please?" asked Beth,
ready to share the lecture.

"You're a dear, and nothing else," answered Meg warmly; and no one
contradicted her, for the "Mouse" was the pet of the family.
